question: In late November 2025, the Spanish Government declared that the tender for the central administration’s cybersecurity contract had been unsuccessful. The tender – to cover the interconnection of central administration data centres and the provision of cybersecurity services – attracted only one bid.

Yet the government excluded that bid because one of the companies involved had more than 50 employees but did not have a registered an equality plan. Months earlier, for the same reason, the Government disqualified another company that had already been declared the winner of the same tender. Spain is one of the Member States most exposed to hybrid threats and cyberattacks.
The contract, which could prove critical to the cybersecurity of the Spanish central administration, will now be delayed by several more months. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission concerned that a project of this scale, which is vital to the cybersecurity of the Spanish administration, is facing months of delay?
Does it believe that mandatory registration of an equality plan by bidding companies is important to safeguarding a country’s cybersecurity?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.2.2026) Directive (EU) 2022/25551 aims to increase the cybersecurity of entities operating in eighteen critical sectors, including public administration.

Under this Directive, Member States must ensure that certain public administration entities have to take cybersecurity risk-management measures, including concerning security in network and information systems acquisition and supply chain security.

Further, Directive (EU) 2022/2555 requires Member States to adopt a national cybersecurity strategy which must contain policies on the inclusion and specification of cybersecurityrelated requirements for information and communications technology products and services in public procurement.

Assuming that the award procedure referred to is subject to Directive 2014/24/EU2, the Commission considers that national courts and review bodies laid down under the Directives on remedies in public procurement3 are in the best position to assess, according to the facts of each case, whether contracting authorities and contracting entities have respected their obligations under EU law.
1 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on measures

for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union (NIS 2 Directive) (OJ L 333, 27.12.2022, p. 80). 2 Directive (EU) 2014/24 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 February 2014 on public procurement and repealing Directive 2004/18/EC (OJ L 94, 28.3.2014, pp. 65–242).

3 In the case at hand, Council Directive (EEC) 89/665 of 21 December 1989 on the coordination of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions relating to the application of review procedures to the award of public supply and public works contracts (OJ L 395 30.12.1989, p. 33).
